title: 2 Life-Changing Words Great Teachers Say Every Day November 7, 2026
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin contends that education has drifted toward naming problems rather than solving them, and that the growing vocabulary of labels, diagnoses and acronyms hands teachers a ready-made excuse for any badly behaved class. He sets great teachers apart as those who refuse to be defined by the labels attached to the students on their roster. His claim is that human children cannot have changed as quickly as the labels suggest, and that what has changed is how the educational establishment views ordinary variation in ability and attention. In his view most differences are not disorders, and students generally respond well to good, clear instruction, so the two words that matter are Don't care, meaning the teacher will teach every child up regardless. He concedes that some students have weak skills and short attention spans, but attributes this to habits shaped by social media, video games, soft parenting and poor teaching, which he says can be reversed. The piece closes by challenging teachers to decide whether they will take the same stance. It is a forceful opinion piece and its blanket skepticism toward diagnoses is the author's view, not an established finding.
points: Linsin argues that a proliferation of labels gives teachers ready-made excuses for poor classroom outcomes.
He holds that most variation in ability and attention reflects bad habits and weak instruction rather than disorders, and that clear teaching serves nearly all students.
The titular two words, Don't care, express a teacher's decision to teach every student up regardless of the label on the file.
The piece treats a teacher's belief in students' capacity to learn as the deciding factor, citing years of first-hand classroom experience.
quotes: Over the past decade the focus of education has shifted more and more toward problems rather than solutions. We’re now conditioned to point to every challenge and say, “See, see, see?!
There are teachers, veteran and rookie alike, who see these labels for what they are. They understand that through all of human history, children cannot possibly change so quickly and drastically.
Yes, of course the smart phone has made a negative impact on learning. No doubt. But what has changed isn’t so much the students. It’s how the failing educational establishment views them.
They’re able to grasp that most differences in ability, attention, etc. aren’t disorders and that all students respond well to good, clear instruction.
Great teachers sweep it all aside and decide for themselves. Because they believe in their students and their capacity to learn if provided the right tools and mindset.

Yes, some have terrible academic skills, the attention span of goldfish, and low motivation due to social media, video games, soft parenting, bad teaching, and the like. But these aren’t disorders. They’re bad habits that can be reversed.
Here at SCM, we talk a lot about how the frightening ease of attaching labels to students has profoundly hurt them and their future.
